subject: Pricing for labeling services
text:
Hi Arisha,

I just at an engineering retreat and got the opportunity to talk to some higher ups about future annotation needs. Like most things, it ultimately comes down to cost. I was wondering if I could get some cost
 estimates for labeling services for the following:

• 
Non-expert annotators. Annotators who don’t have any medical accreditation/certification but are familiar with the Encord platform. I believe the expectation
 is that they would be able to pass a training relevant to the assigned task. Some possible tasks would be labeling fundus images as good or bad quality, likely with optional details like “smudge on image”, “out of focus”, “overexposed”. We also might be interested
 in non-expert graders labeling presence of specific biomarkers which we would have reviewed by a medical expert (either internal or external).

• 
Ophthalmologist or optometrists expert annotators. Annotators with experience diagnosing eye diseases based on retinal fundus imaging and ideally have
 a relevant accreditation/certification. For these graders we would primarily be assigning tasks to label presence of eye diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, age related macular degeneration (AMD), and possibly of glaucoma (cannot be diagnosed definitively
 from a fundus image). We would likely need to have more discussion with an expert grading to make sure we have agreement on the grading standard used for a given disease.

I’m also interested in more general questions:

• 
Is it generally hourly or fixed per number of tasks?

• 
Are there volume minimums?

• 
How are rejected annotations handled?

• 
What does a typical training project look like?

I don’t believe there is urgency on these questions. If more discussion is needed maybe we could go over it during our next meeting on October 16th? I will give a caveat that I don’t personally
 have any decision-making power and would likely need to pass any questions along. I can always try to pull a manager or director into a meeting

subject: RE: Pricing for labeling services
text:
Hi Arisha and Alyssa,

I just added 3 example projects with accelerate@encord.com<mailto:accelerate@encord.com> as a manger. For each project I did one annotation that is in Review as an example. We don’t have annotation instruction PDFs (we can make them) but I’ll list the standards in these examples:

  1.  Example expert grading | Encord<https://app.encord.com/projects/view/5aca702f-9080-4bbc-afec-a123eae80f93/settings> – This is the type of project we would want an eye care professional to grade. It includes labeling:
     *   Diabetic retinopathy (DR) severity with options - [“less than moderate”, “moderate”, “vision threatening”, “ungradable”]. If talking to a doctor I believe we use a standard of ETDRS level 35 or above for *moderate*, not sure for vision threatening.
     *   Diabetic macular edema (DME) presence - True/False. If talking to a doctor, either center involved or non-center involved DME.
     *   Image Quality – whether the image is good quality, binary Good/Bad. This is distinct from “ungradable” because an image can be very low quality but if disease is obvious it may still be gradable. This is something we also have non-expert graders label
     *   Laser scaring – whether there is visible laser scaring from past treatment for DR, binary True/False. We also would potentially have non-experts label this.
  2.  Non-expert objects annotation | Encord<https://app.encord.com/projects/view/43285f5c-ff4f-427b-aac3-825afd12541e/summary> – This is a project we would have a non-expert annotate the location of specific biomarkers/landmarks in a fundus image
     *   Fovea center – center of fovea landmark [see example]
     *   Optic disc (OD) center – center of optic disk landmark
     *   Fixation – which landmark is in the center of the image: [“Fovea”, “OD”, “Center”, “Unknown”] where “Center” means between the OD and fovea, and Unknown is anything not in the list.

subject: Re: Encord Python 3.8 Deprecation
text:
Hi Arisha and friends! Thanks for the meeting earlier today - we've had a
look at your suggestions, and our codebase, and we may be in need of some
more guidance.

We use QueueRunners, not SequentialRunners, in our workflow. We can try to
update our QueueRunners to return TaskAgentReturnStructs, but it seems most
of these recommended changes apply more to SequentialRunners. Can you
provide an example using QueueRunners? The example provided here
<https://docs.encord.com/agents-documentation/Task-Agents/Execution/Multi-Processing>
uses
QueueRunners to set the priority of a given LabelRowV2, and it's not far
off from our implementation. Our understanding is that if this were to be
run using something like Celery, and there were 1000 items in the stage, it
would result in 1000 independent API calls.

In addition, our tasks typically require the raw frame to perform
inference. If the raw frame is sourced from Encord from within an
independent process, we're not sure how to bundle those downloads using
QueueRunners either. We can get the data_link from the LabelRowV2 and
download it from S3 ourselves, but it seems to us that getting the
data_link would still constitute an API call.

We also had a look at the source here
<https://github.com/encord-team/encord-agents/blob/main/encord_agents/tasks/runner/queue_runner.py>
and
it seems that bundling isn't supported for the QueueRunner. We even see a
comment at line 214 (# Can't batch handle updates for Queue Runner).

Is there a sustainable way to A: minimize calls to your APIs with bundling
and B: Continue using QueueRunners so that we can continue to make use of
our existing infrastructure for parallel inference?

Daniel

text:
Yes, that works for me.

Some context for the discussion:

Currently, I have a lot of annotated images, but I have even more non-annotated images, and I am looking for efficient ways to help me scale operations. I am wondering if the Index/Active modules could help improve the process for target sampling from a large dataset of non-annotated exams (some of these quality issues are like a needle in a haystack), or maybe even help by pre-annotating images for certain labels/objects. I remember seeing something similar in the prior Active demo - if I recall correctly, they used annotations to fine tune SAM or SAM2 to find other non-annotated images that may be similar, and the model outlined the bodies of water.

Anyway, I am hoping on Monday, you can remind me what is possible with Index/Active and what is not. I am guessing we still have the limitation of having to convert to a PNG, but I think that can work for some criteria as long as it does not significantly impact quality and the output is cleared by the Densitas algo team.

I also would like to strategize for the team demo, if possible. It would be excellent if we could use our mammo data and search for something like implants or pacemakers (something easy to spot). Maybe that is not possible but hoping we can find something to demonstrate the usefulness and the need to switch from our current sampling/markup strategy.

Anyway, once we touch base quickly, we can schedule some time with the rest of the team.

See you next week!

Thanks again,
Nicole

subject: Re: Encord features
text:
Hi,

Sorry for the delay in my response.
Thank you Arisha for your video, it is very insightful. I will be
implementing the step pushing bounding boxes with a predefined height.

These two requests were part of a workflow for ECG annotations. An
annotator is asked to select windows (which are annotated by other
annotators) from two ECG leads (2 rows) displayed like in the screenshot
attached. The two leads being related, an event happening in one row is
supposed to happen at the same moment in the second row. The window
selection in either row should be the same. Enforcing the boxes to cover
the whole window would prevent annotators from trying to annotate the 2
leads independently.
[image: image.png]
In another annotation step, annotators are asked to select specific points
on the signal. This step is display dependent: the displayed signal might
be covered with noise, therefore one might be tempted to zoom in, in an
attempt to place more "accurately" the points. If another annotator does
not zoom in, he/she might place the point a little further away which
reduces the consensus between annotators.

Best regards,
Nicolas
